# The suite's rules

Every `mvn test` checks the rules below before any test opens a browser, whichever tests were asked
for (BaseTest does, once per run; no test runs while one is broken). It reads the sources: no
browser, well under a second. **SuiteRulesTest** reports them, **one entry per rule**, so a failure
names the rule it broke (`SR-07 A story has one check`) and says what is wrong, in which file (and
line, where there is one), why the rule exists, and how to fix it.

The rules are **strict on purpose**. They are what keeps the suite readable and trustworthy while
many hands change it: people in a hurry, and AIs that write tests from stories and may half-remember
the conventions. They can't be switched off or edited in the suite: SuiteRules.java, SuiteRulesTest.java
and this file are regenerated with the suite, and SR-16 fails if any of them (or any other generated
file) is changed outside its YOURS blocks. To change a rule, change Suite Builder.

| Rule | What must be true |
| --- | --- |
| [SR-01](#sr-01--every-test-is-in-cases) | Every test is in cases/ |
| [SR-02](#sr-02--every-test-stands-on-basetest-a-story-on-storytest) | Every test stands on BaseTest (a story on StoryTest) |
| [SR-03](#sr-03--a-story-names-its-story) | A story names its story |
| [SR-04](#sr-04--a-story-class-is-named-after-its-id) | A story class is named after its id |
| [SR-05](#sr-05--each-story-id-is-used-once) | Each story id is used once |
| [SR-06](#sr-06--a-story-is-one-test) | A story is one test |
| [SR-07](#sr-07--a-story-has-one-check) | A story has one check |
| [SR-08](#sr-08--the-check-comes-last) | The check comes last |
| [SR-09](#sr-09--a-storys-test-reads-as-its-title) | A story's test reads as its title |
| [SR-10](#sr-10--a-story-uses-page-objects-not-playwright) | A story uses page objects, not Playwright |
| [SR-11](#sr-11--a-story-does-not-assert) | A story does not assert |
| [SR-12](#sr-12--nothing-sleeps) | Nothing sleeps |
| [SR-13](#sr-13--no-regular-expressions-in-tests-and-pages) | No regular expressions in tests and pages |
| [SR-14](#sr-14--no-test-is-switched-off) | No test is switched off |
| [SR-15](#sr-15--yours-blocks-keep-both-marker-lines) | YOURS blocks keep both marker lines |
| [SR-16](#sr-16--generated-files-change-only-inside-yours-blocks) | Generated files change only inside YOURS blocks |
| [SR-17](#sr-17--every-story-in-storiesdone-has-its-test) | Every story in stories/done/ has its test |
| [SR-18](#sr-18--every-story-test-has-its-story-in-storiesdone) | Every story test has its story in stories/done/ |
| [SR-19](#sr-19--every-test-checks-something) | Every test checks something |

A **story** is a class in `cases/` that Suite Builder did not generate (it is not in
`src/test/resources/suite-rules/fingerprints.txt`), or any test carrying
`@Story` or extending `StoryTest`. SR-03 to SR-11 are about stories; the rest hold for every test.

Run just the rules: `mvn test -Dtest=SuiteRulesTest` (in xoveconsulting-com-tests).

## Sealed

These rules are the tests of the tests, and they are **off limits** to people and AIs alike. When a
rule fails, the test is what is wrong (or the story it came from): never the rule. Changing a rules
file, taking out its first lines, skipping SuiteRulesTest or weakening BaseTest's check to get a
test through is tampering, and it is caught three ways:

- **SR-16**, in every run, compares each generated file with its fingerprint.
- **Every rebuild** (`suite build xoveconsulting-com-tests`) rewrites SuiteRules.java, SuiteRulesTest.java, HarnessTest.java, this
  file and the fingerprints whole, whatever they say about themselves, regenerates every other
  generated file outside its YOURS blocks, and lists what it put back.
- **`suite verify xoveconsulting-com-tests`**, from Suite Builder, compares every generated file with what
  the tool itself generates from the project's crawl. Unlike SR-16 it can't be fooled by editing a
  rule and its fingerprint together. `suite test xoveconsulting-com-tests` puts back what was changed, then
  runs `mvn test`.

**HarnessTest** is sealed with them: it tests the suite's own machinery (that a failure leaves its
evidence, that every check passes and fails as it should, with the message a person reads, that
every action does what its step says) on a page it writes itself, with every run. When it fails,
the harness is broken, not the site.

On a team, make it stick: run `suite verify` in CI before `mvn test`, and have the rules
files reviewed by their owner, e.g. in `.github/CODEOWNERS` (with branch protection on):

```
SUITE-RULES.md                  @your-qa-lead
**/SuiteRules.java              @your-qa-lead
**/SuiteRulesTest.java          @your-qa-lead
**/BaseTest.java                @your-qa-lead
pom.xml                         @your-qa-lead
src/test/resources/suite-rules/fingerprints.txt  @your-qa-lead
```

## SR-01 · Every test is in cases/

**What it checks.** Every class under src/test/java with a test method (@Test, @TestFactory, @ParameterizedTest, @RepeatedTest or @TestTemplate), apart from the suite's own tests (SuiteRulesTest and HarnessTest), is in the cases/ folder (its package ends in .cases).

**Why.** One folder holds every test, generated or written from a story, and nothing else. A person looking for tests finds all of them there, and can delete a stale story without touching the machinery the tests stand on (BaseTest, StoryTest, Story, the rules), which is one folder up.

**How to fix it.** Move the class into cases/ and change its package line to &lt;base>.cases. Import what it uses from one level up (BaseTest, StoryTest, Story).

Breaks the rule:

```java
// src/test/java/com/example/tests/stories/Engi101.java
package com.example.tests.stories;
```

Follows it:

```java
// src/test/java/com/example/tests/cases/Engi101.java
package com.example.tests.cases;

import com.example.tests.Story;
import com.example.tests.StoryTest;
```

## SR-02 · Every test stands on BaseTest (a story on StoryTest)

**What it checks.** A class with tests extends BaseTest, directly or through another class; a story (a class in cases/ that the suite did not generate, or one carrying @Story) extends StoryTest.

**Why.** BaseTest is what gives a test its browser, its numbered plain-English step log, and the evidence of a failure (screenshot, the page's HTML, a trace). StoryTest adds the story's id to the log. A test that stands on neither runs blind and fails without a word of why.

**How to fix it.** Write "extends StoryTest" for a story, "extends BaseTest" for any other test.

Breaks the rule:

```java
class Engi101 {
```

Follows it:

```java
class Engi101 extends StoryTest {
```

## SR-03 · A story names its story

**What it checks.** A story class carries @Story with the story's id: @Story(value = "engi-101", title = "...").

**Why.** The id ties the test to the story in the team's tracker and in stories/done/: the run log prints it, a failure points back to it, and SR-17 and SR-18 check the two stay together.

**How to fix it.** Put @Story(value = "&lt;id>", title = "&lt;the story's title>") above the class, the id exactly as the story writes it.

Breaks the rule:

```java
class Engi101 extends StoryTest {
```

Follows it:

```java
@Story(value = "engi-101", title = "Learn More on the home page leads to Careers")
class Engi101 extends StoryTest {
```

## SR-04 · A story class is named after its id

**What it checks.** The class name is the @Story id with its letters and digits kept and the first made upper case: engi-101 is Engi101, INJ-592 is INJ592. An id that starts with a digit gets "Story" in front.

**Why.** Anyone holding a story id finds its test by name, in cases/, without searching: that is what makes a stale story easy to delete. The file is named after the class, as Java requires.

**How to fix it.** Rename the class (and its file) to the name the message gives.

Breaks the rule:

```java
@Story(value = "engi-101", title = "...")
class LearnMoreTest extends StoryTest {
```

Follows it:

```java
@Story(value = "engi-101", title = "...")
class Engi101 extends StoryTest {
```

## SR-05 · Each story id is used once

**What it checks.** No two story classes carry the same @Story id (capitals aside).

**Why.** One story, one test: a second class with the same id is a copy that drifts from the first, and deleting "the" test of a stale story leaves the other behind.

**How to fix it.** Keep one class per id. If the two check different things, they are two stories: give the second its own id and story file.

## SR-06 · A story is one test

**What it checks.** A story class has exactly one test method, of any kind JUnit runs (@Test, @TestFactory, @ParameterizedTest, @RepeatedTest, @TestTemplate): a parameterized test is one test run many times, each run its own outcome.

**Why.** A story is one visitor's journey with one outcome. Two tests in one story class are two outcomes, and the story that asked for both was two stories: splitting them keeps each failure pointing at one thing.

**How to fix it.** Keep the one test for the story's outcome. Anything else it checked is another story: write it up (stories/new/) and let it get its own class.

Breaks the rule:

```java
class Engi101 extends StoryTest {
    @Test void learnMore() { ... }
    @Test void applyNow() { ... }
}
```

Follows it:

```java
@Story(value = "engi-101", title = "Learn More on the home page leads to Careers")
class Engi101 extends StoryTest {

    @Test
    @DisplayName("Learn More on the home page leads to Careers")
    void story() {
        new HomePage(page).open()
                .click().learnMore()
                .verify().isLoaded();
    }
}
```

## SR-07 · A story has one check

**What it checks.** A story class calls .verify() exactly once.

**Why.** "One verify per story" (Ghost, 2026-09-28): a story states one outcome, and its test proves that one. A story with two checks was badly written and gets pushed back (stories/AI-INSTRUCTIONS.md). Arriving on a page needs no check of its own: every page checks it has loaded when a step lands on it.

**How to fix it.** No verify(): end the chain with the check the story's outcome asks for. Two or more: the story has two outcomes; push back and split it into stories.

Breaks the rule:

```java
.click().learnMore()
.verify().headingMentions("Careers")
...
.verify().showsTheJobSection();
```

Follows it:

```java
.click().learnMore()
.verify().isLoaded();
```

## SR-08 · The check comes last

**What it checks.** After a story's .verify(), nothing else is done: no click(), enter(), check(), uncheck(), clear(), read(), execute(), navigateTo() or open().

**Why.** The check is the story's outcome, so the story ends there. A step after it is either a second outcome in disguise, or a step the check did not cover.

**How to fix it.** Move the steps before the verify(), or if they lead to a second outcome, make that a story of its own.

Breaks the rule:

```java
.verify().isLoaded()
.click().applyNow();
```

Follows it:

```java
.click().applyNow()
.verify().showsTheJobSection();
```

## SR-09 · A story's test reads as its title

**What it checks.** The story's @Test carries @DisplayName("...").

**Why.** The report and the run log show the display name: with the story's title there, a person who never opens the code reads which story passed or failed.

**How to fix it.** Put @DisplayName("&lt;the story's title>") on the test.

## SR-10 · A story uses page objects, not Playwright

**What it checks.** A story class does not import com.microsoft.playwright, call .locator( or .getBy..., or call the page itself (page.): it goes through page objects.

**Why.** A story reads like the story because every step is a page method named for what a visitor does ("click().learnMore()"). Locators and browser calls in a test hide what it does, break when the site changes in many places at once, and skip the step log and the waits the page objects give.

**How to fix it.** Add the element to the page's Elements enum (ai/recipes/add-an-element.md) and an action or check that uses it (add-an-action.md); call that from the story.

Breaks the rule:

```java
page.locator("xpath=//a[@aria-label='Learn More']").click();
```

Follows it:

```java
new HomePage(page).open()
        .click().learnMore()
```

## SR-11 · A story does not assert

**What it checks.** A story class uses no assertions: no assert, assertTrue/assertEquals/assertFalse/assertThat, Assertions., fail(.

**Why.** Checks live in the pages' verify() methods, built on Checks, which log the step and fail in plain English ("Expected the email input to hold ..."). An assertion in a story fails with "expected true", logs nothing, and is a second check SR-07 cannot see.

**How to fix it.** Add the check to the page's VerifyActions (ai/recipes/add-an-action.md) and end the chain with verify().&lt;that check>.

Breaks the rule:

```java
assertTrue(page.url().endsWith("/careers"));
```

Follows it:

```java
.verify().isLoaded();
```

## SR-12 · Nothing sleeps

**What it checks.** No Thread.sleep( or waitForTimeout( (a sleep by another name) anywhere in the tests and pages (core/ aside), and no shortenWaits( outside the suite's own harness.

**Why.** A sleep is too long on a fast day and too short on a slow one: the test gets slower and still flaky. WaitActions waits for the thing itself (an element to show or go away, a URL), exactly as long as needed.

**How to fix it.** Wait for what the step needs with WaitActions (ai/recipes/wait-for-a-slow-page.md).

Breaks the rule:

```java
Thread.sleep(2000);
```

Follows it:

```java
WaitActions.waitForInvisibilityOf(page, HomeElements.LOADING_SPINNER);
```

## SR-13 · No regular expressions in tests and pages

**What it checks.** No java.util.regex, Pattern.compile, .matches(, .replaceAll(, .replaceFirst( or .split( in the tests and pages (core/ aside): each of the last four takes a regular expression.

**Why.** Tests and pages are read and changed by people who aren't programmers; a regular expression is where they stop understanding. Plain strings say what they mean.

**How to fix it.** Compare plain strings (Checks.hasText, containsText; WaitActions.sameText). If a pattern is truly needed, put it in a helper in core/ with a plain name, and call that.

## SR-14 · No test is switched off

**What it checks.** No @Disabled in the tests, and nothing in pom.xml that switches tests off or ignores their failures: skipTests, maven.test.skip, testFailureIgnore, skipAfterFailureCount, an &lt;excludes> list.

**Why.** A switched-off test hides a failure and is forgotten. A test that no longer applies is deleted; one that fails because of the site is a known issue, recorded in KNOWN-ISSUES.md where people see it. Switching tests off in the pom (its YOURS blocks allow properties) would silence the whole suite, these rules included, while mvn test still says BUILD SUCCESS.

**How to fix it.** Delete the test (a stale story: its class in cases/ and its file in stories/done/), or fix it, or record the site's fault in KNOWN-ISSUES.md. Take the setting out of pom.xml; to run fewer tests for a while, say so on the command line (-Dgroups=smoke, -Dtest=...), where it lasts one run.

## SR-15 · YOURS blocks keep both marker lines

**What it checks.** Every file has as many YOURS opening lines as closing ones, counting only marker lines that are comments (starting with //, &lt;!-- or #): exactly the lines regenerating reads as markers.

**Why.** Regenerating keeps what is between a block's two marker lines, and only that. With a marker gone, whatever was in the block is lost the next time the suite is regenerated.

**How to fix it.** Put the missing line back exactly as it was: // ==== YOURS (name): ... ==== and // ==== END YOURS (name) ====.

## SR-16 · Generated files change only inside YOURS blocks

**What it checks.** Every file Suite Builder generated (listed with a fingerprint in src/test/resources/suite-rules/fingerprints.txt) is still there, and its text outside the YOURS blocks is exactly as generated. That includes the rules themselves: SuiteRules.java, SuiteRulesTest.java and SUITE-RULES.md.

**Why.** Regenerating the suite (a new crawl of a changed site) rewrites everything outside YOURS blocks, so a change made there silently disappears. And the rules are only worth something if nobody, person or AI, can quietly edit or delete them to make a failing test pass.

**How to fix it.** Move your change into a YOURS block or a file of your own, and put the rest back: regenerating restores it (suite build &lt;project>, which keeps everything in YOURS blocks). To change a rule, change Suite Builder, not the generated suite.

## SR-17 · Every story in stories/done/ has its test

**What it checks.** For each story file in stories/done/ (README.md aside), a story class carries its id in @Story. The id is the first word shaped like INJ-592 in the file name, else in the story's text above any ---- line, else the file name.

**Why.** stories/done/ is the record of which stories the suite checks. A story there without a test claims coverage that isn't there.

**How to fix it.** Implement the story (stories/AI-INSTRUCTIONS.md), or move it back to stories/new/, or, if it is stale, delete it.

## SR-18 · Every story test has its story in stories/done/

**What it checks.** For each story class, a story file in stories/done/ has its @Story id.

**Why.** The story file is the test's reason to exist, in the words of whoever asked for it; without it nobody can tell whether the test still checks something wanted. Together with SR-17 it means a stale story is retired by deleting both, and forgetting one is caught.

**How to fix it.** Add the story to stories/done/ (its words, with the IMPLEMENTED note naming this class), or, if the story is stale, delete this class too.

## SR-19 · Every test checks something

**What it checks.** Every test method (@Test, @ParameterizedTest, @RepeatedTest; the generated tests' too) checks at least one thing: a .verify() chain, a Checks call, or an assertion, in the method itself or in a method of the same class it calls (helper() or this.helper()). A story is held to exactly one .verify() by SR-07 instead.

**Why.** A test that only acts (opens a page, clicks a link) and checks nothing passes whenever nothing throws: it can't tell the right page from the wrong one, and a green run says less than it seems. Even the plainest test ends by saying what it expected, if only that the page it reached has loaded (Ghost, 2026-09-28).

**How to fix it.** End the test with the check it is for: .verify().isLoaded() on the page it reaches at the least, or a Checks call (Checks.isOnPath for a page with no page class).

Breaks the rule:

```java
new HomePage(page).open()
        .click().goToAbout();
```

Follows it:

```java
new HomePage(page).open()
        .click().goToAbout()
        .verify().isLoaded();
```
